channel.title: Clinical on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Clinical on Best of AI

item.title: Airfinity
item.description:
Airfinity provides data and forecasts about health threats and the products to counter them. Its analysts and models track outbreaks, monitor vaccine and drug development pipelines, and estimate supply, demand, and production. The data helps decision makers judge where a disease is heading and which products might reach the market.

The company became widely known for its work during the COVID-19 pandemic, when it tracked vaccine production and distribution around the world, and has since expanded to other diseases and to wider life sciences analysis. Its customers include pharmaceutical companies planning strategy, investors, public health bodies, and policy groups. Machine learning helps process large volumes of data from many sources.

item.title: AliveCor
item.description:
AliveCor makes consumer and clinical ECG tools. The KardiaMobile devices are small sensors that you touch with your fingers while a phone app records a single-lead or multi-lead electrocardiogram. The app uses algorithms cleared by regulators in many regions to say whether the rhythm looks normal, shows atrial fibrillation, or is unclassified.

Records can be saved, shared with a doctor, and compared over time. People with palpitations or a history of arrhythmia use it to capture an episode as it happens, and clinicians use it to monitor patients remotely. The company also offers a subscription that adds more analysis, reports, and access to cardiologist review.

item.title: Ambience Healthcare
item.description:
Ambience builds AI for the paperwork around medical care. With patient consent, its system captures the conversation between clinician and patient, then generates a structured note in the clinician’s preferred format. The clinician reviews and signs it, which cuts the time spent charting after hours.

Its distinct focus is coding and compliance. From the same conversation and the chart, the tool suggests diagnosis and procedure codes with supporting evidence, which can reduce missed codes and billing errors. Because of that, it targets health systems and large practices rather than single clinicians, and it works with different specialties.

item.title: DeepScribe
item.description:
DeepScribe is an ambient scribe for doctors. With the patient’s consent, the system listens during the visit, separates the conversation from small talk, and produces a structured note in the format a specialty expects. The clinician edits and signs it in the electronic health record.

The company started with oncology, where notes are long and complex, and has expanded to other outpatient fields. Beyond notes, it helps capture details needed for coding and quality reporting, and works with major record systems so notes appear where doctors expect them. The goal is to give clinicians their evenings back.

item.title: ImageTrend
item.description:
ImageTrend makes software for first responders. Paramedics and EMTs record patient information, treatments, and outcomes on a tablet or computer, producing the report used for handoff to hospitals, billing, and quality review. The data also feeds state and national registries.

The company also provides tools for state EMS offices, trauma and stroke registries, and hospital data collection, as well as analytics for system performance. Newer tools use AI to help reduce documentation time and check data quality.

item.title: IQVIA
item.description:
IQVIA sits at the center of the pharmaceutical industry’s information flow. It collects and sells data on prescriptions, healthcare utilization, and patient activity from a large number of sources, which companies use to understand markets, size opportunities, and plan commercial strategy. The company is also a major contract research organization that runs clinical trials, recruiting patients, managing sites, and handling data on behalf of drug developers.

Technology and AI are applied to both lines of business. Analytics platforms combine data sets to deliver insights to sales and marketing teams, and AI helps identify suitable trial sites and patients, predict enrollment, and automate documentation and safety reporting. IQVIA has been building AI agents for tasks such as data analysis and trial operations, often in partnership with large technology companies.

item.title: iRhythm
item.description:
iRhythm provides a way to monitor heart rhythm over a longer time than a short office test. A doctor prescribes the Zio patch, which is a small adhesive device placed on the chest. It records every heartbeat for up to two weeks while the patient goes about normal life, then is mailed back for analysis.

The company’s software uses deep learning to analyze the recording and flag events such as atrial fibrillation, pauses, and other arrhythmias. Certified technicians and clinicians then review the findings and create a report for the physician. This approach catches intermittent problems that a brief ECG would miss, and helps guide treatment decisions.

item.title: MyTherapy
item.description:
MyTherapy is a free medication reminder app. Users enter their drugs and schedule, receive alerts at the right times, and confirm each dose. The app also tracks health values such as blood pressure and weight, and records symptoms and mood, which builds a picture of how treatment is going.

Reports summarize adherence and measurements, giving doctors useful data at appointments. Family members can be set up to follow along, which helps those who care for relatives. The app supports many languages.

item.title: Notable
item.description:
Notable automates administrative work in healthcare. Its agents reach out to patients by text, phone, or app to schedule visits, collect forms, confirm insurance, and manage referrals, and they write the results into the health record. The goal is to free staff from repetitive tasks and improve patient access.

Integration is the key difference: agents work inside systems like Epic and others, performing steps in the same workflows staff use. Health systems deploy them for areas such as pre-visit intake, care gap outreach, and prior authorization support.

item.title: Veeva Systems
item.description:
Veeva is the dominant software vendor for pharmaceutical companies. Its CRM supports sales and medical teams that engage with physicians, Vault is a cloud platform for managing documents and processes in areas such as clinical operations, regulatory submissions, quality, and safety, and data products supply information about healthcare providers and markets. Companies use these tools to run regulated, document-heavy processes.

The company has been adding AI across its applications. Veeva AI agents help users search content, prepare documents, and automate steps such as drafting summaries or checking submissions, built into Vault and its CRM and operating under the industry’s compliance requirements. It has also moved its CRM off the Salesforce platform onto its own technology.

item.title: BlueDot
item.description:
BlueDot is an epidemic intelligence company. Its system scans huge volumes of text and data, including news in many languages, animal disease reports, and travel patterns, looking for signs of unusual outbreaks. Epidemiologists review the signals and issue alerts with analysis.

The company drew attention when it flagged the cluster of pneumonia cases that became COVID-19 before many official announcements. Flight data helps estimate where infected travelers might go, which supports early warnings to governments, airlines, and health organizations.

item.title: Cardiologs
item.description:
Cardiologs applies AI to heart rhythm recordings. Technicians and cardiologists traditionally spend hours reviewing long ECG tracings, such as 24-hour or multi-day Holter recordings. The software analyzes the signal, classifies heartbeats and rhythms, and highlights segments that need attention so reviewers can concentrate on them.

Reports summarize findings, including atrial fibrillation burden, pauses, and other events, in a form the physician can verify and edit. The tool works with data from different monitoring devices and integrates into clinical workflows. Philips acquired the company to add ECG analysis to its cardiac monitoring portfolio.

item.title: Freed
item.description:
Freed helps clinicians finish notes faster. During a visit, with patient consent, it records the conversation and produces a structured note in a familiar format, which the clinician reviews, edits, and copies into the record. It also drafts instructions for the patient.

It is popular with independent practitioners, such as physicians, nurse practitioners, and therapists, because it is easy to set up and priced for individuals. Features include templates by specialty, custom note styles, and a learning feature that adapts to how a clinician writes.

item.title: Glass Health
item.description:
Glass Health helps with clinical reasoning and documentation. A clinician enters or dictates a patient summary, and the assistant proposes a list of possible diagnoses, along with reasoning and suggested next steps. A plan builder drafts assessment and plan sections, and reference citations let the user check where claims come from.

It also supports note writing, and a library of clinical guidelines and content supports decisions. Physicians, residents, and students use it to think through cases and save time on write-ups. The product emphasizes that the clinician stays responsible for decisions.

item.title: Hippocratic AI
item.description:
Hippocratic AI focuses on non-diagnostic work in healthcare. Its agents call patients to check on recovery after discharge, remind them to take medication, prepare them for procedures, and monitor chronic conditions. The calls are long, patient conversations that clinical staff rarely have time to make.

Safety is the stated priority. The company tests its models with clinicians and designs the agents to stay within defined roles, escalating to a nurse or doctor when a patient reports symptoms that need attention. Health systems deploy them to extend staff capacity and reach patients between visits.

item.title: Jane
item.description:
Jane is practice management software for health and wellness clinics. Patients book online, receive reminders, and pay through the system, while practitioners chart visits, manage insurance billing, and run reports. A telehealth feature supports virtual visits.

The AI assistant helps with documentation. A clinician dictates or types notes, and Jane structures them into a SOAP note, saving time at the end of the day. Multi-practitioner clinics can manage schedules, rooms, and staff in one place.

item.title: LeanTaaS
item.description:
LeanTaaS builds software for healthcare capacity. Hospitals struggle with uneven demand: operating rooms sit idle while patients wait, infusion chairs are overbooked on some days, and beds are not available when needed. LeanTaaS forecasts demand and recommends schedules that balance resources and reduce wait times.

Its iQueue products cover operating rooms, infusion centers, and inpatient beds. Algorithms assess historical patterns and help staff adjust block time, appointment slots, and staffing. Improvements can increase the number of patients served without adding space.

item.title: Medidata
item.description:
Medidata is a major provider of clinical trial technology. Rave Electronic Data Capture collects patient data from trial sites, and other products handle randomization, imaging, patient-reported outcomes, and trial planning. Pharmaceutical companies and research organizations use the platform to run studies from start to finish.

AI and analytics help trial teams. Models flag sites with unusual data, predict enrollment problems, and help design studies using historical trial data, and the company has built synthetic control arm methods that use past patients to supplement studies. These aim to make trials faster and more efficient.

item.title: Medisafe
item.description:
Medisafe helps people take medicines as prescribed. Users enter their medications, get reminders at the right time, and log doses. If a dose is missed, the app follows up, and caregivers can be notified. Interaction checks warn about conflicts between drugs when a new one is added.

Programs with pharmacies, health plans, and drugmakers build on the app, offering support for particular conditions and tracking adherence. Features include refill reminders, health measurement tracking, and educational content. AI helps personalize reminders and detect patterns.

item.title: Qventus
item.description:
Qventus works on hospital operations. It connects to scheduling and records systems, forecasts demand in the emergency room, operating rooms, and inpatient units, and flags bottlenecks like discharges that are running late or beds that will not be ready. It recommends actions for staff.

Automation is part of the pitch. The platform can complete tasks like reaching out to patients for scheduling or following up on referrals, and AI agents handle routine work in areas such as surgical scheduling and call centers. The goal is to improve access while easing staff burden.

item.title: Careforce AI
item.description:
Careforce provides AI workers for healthcare administration. Agents place outbound calls and texts to patients, such as to schedule overdue screenings, confirm appointments, and collect information before a visit. They handle follow-up and rescheduling, which often falls through in busy offices.

The company says its agents support many languages and can work across scheduling systems and payer portals, which lets clinics reach patients who might otherwise be missed. Scripts are configurable for different campaigns, such as preventive care outreach and post-operative check-ins.

item.title: Heidi Health
item.description:
Heidi is an AI scribe for clinicians. During a visit, with the patient’s consent, it records and transcribes the conversation, then generates a note in the structure the clinician prefers, such as SOAP or a specialty template. The clinician reviews and edits before saving it to the record.

Beyond notes, it can write letters, patient instructions, and other documents from the same consultation, and supports multiple languages. Heidi began in Australia and has grown internationally, with a free tier that made it popular with individual practitioners alongside plans for clinics and health systems.

item.title: OpenEvidence
item.description:
OpenEvidence works like a medical search engine that writes answers. A clinician asks a question, such as the first-line treatment for a condition or how to manage a drug interaction, and the system searches the medical literature and produces a summary with references to the underlying studies and guidelines.

It has partnerships with major medical publishers and journals, which gives it access to authoritative content. Clinicians use it at the point of care, and it has become widely used among US physicians. The company funds it through advertising aimed at medical professionals.

item.title: ESO
item.description:
ESO makes software for emergency medical services and fire departments. Paramedics record patient information, vitals, treatments, and outcomes on a tablet or laptop, producing the patient care report that is shared with hospitals and used for billing and quality review.

AI helps reduce documentation time. The software can draft narrative sections from the structured data a medic entered, and flag missing or inconsistent items so reports are complete. The company also sells products for hospitals, health data analytics, and fire records management.

item.title: Everbridge
item.description:
Everbridge helps organizations respond when something goes wrong. A hurricane, an active threat, an IT outage, or a supply chain disruption triggers the need to reach employees, residents, or customers quickly. The platform sends alerts by text, voice, email, and app notification, and tracks who has responded.

Its risk intelligence monitors global sources to detect events near offices, facilities, and travelers, and AI helps filter the noise. Organizations can map assets, identify who is affected, and launch response plans. Governments use related tools for public warning systems.

item.title: Pulsara
item.description:
Pulsara speeds time-critical care. A paramedic starts a patient channel from the field, adds vitals and images, and alerts the receiving hospital, so teams can prepare before arrival. Stroke, heart attack, and trauma cases benefit when clinicians coordinate early.

Within the hospital, Pulsara links departments such as the emergency room, imaging, and specialists, and keeps a timeline of communications. The data supports review of response times and quality improvement. AI features assist with transcription and information routing.

item.title: Abridge
item.description: Abridge targets one of healthcare’s biggest burdens: the time doctors spend writing notes. With patient consent, the app records the conversation during a visit, and AI turns it into a structured clinical note in the format the clinician needs, ready for review and insertion into the electronic health record. After the visit, a patient-friendly summary can also be produced. The aim is to let doctors focus on the patient instead of the screen.

item.title: Ada Health
item.description:
Ada guides users through a structured conversation about their symptoms. It asks about what you feel, when it started, your medical history, and related factors, adapting each question based on earlier answers, and then shows possible conditions with likelihoods and recommendations such as self-care, seeing a doctor, or seeking urgent help. The app was developed with doctors and is available in several languages.

The consumer app is free to use, and Ada also licenses its technology to health systems and insurers, who embed it in their own services for triage and navigation. The aim is to help people understand their symptoms, avoid unnecessary visits, and know when something needs prompt attention. Users can share a summary with their clinician.

item.title: Aidoc
item.description:
Aidoc builds AI for radiology workflows. When a scan such as a head CT or chest CT is taken, Aidoc’s algorithms analyze it in the background and, if they detect a suspected critical finding, move the study to the top of the radiologist’s worklist and notify the relevant team. This shortens the time to review urgent cases like intracranial hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, and aortic dissection, where minutes matter.

The company has grown from single-finding triage into a broader platform. It offers an operating system for deploying many algorithms, including those from other developers, and coordinates care for conditions that need multidisciplinary response. Recent work includes foundation models for imaging and tools that combine imaging with clinical data, and a growing number of FDA clearances.

item.title: AlphaFold
item.description: AlphaFold tackled a problem that biologists worked on for fifty years: predicting how a chain of amino acids folds into a three-dimensional protein. Shape determines function, so knowing the structure helps researchers understand diseases, design drugs, and engineer enzymes. Before AlphaFold, determining a structure took expensive experiments such as X-ray crystallography that could take months or years. AlphaFold predicts many structures with accuracy that is often close to experimental results.

item.title: Babylon Health
item.description:
Babylon Health set out to make primary care available through a smartphone. Its app offered an AI-powered symptom checker and chatbot, video consultations with doctors, prescriptions, and health tracking. It partnered with the UK’s National Health Service, ran digital GP services, and expanded to countries including Rwanda and the United States, attracting large investment and a public listing.

The company faced criticism over the safety claims made for its AI, the quality of its services, and its finances. Doctors and researchers questioned how well the chatbot performed in comparison to human clinicians, and contracts with public health systems brought scrutiny. It then ran into financial trouble, and the business went into administration, with parts sold, including its UK operations.

item.title: BenevolentAI
item.description:
BenevolentAI built a platform that gathers large amounts of biomedical information, including scientific literature, clinical data, and experimental results, into a knowledge graph that connects diseases, genes, proteins, and drugs. Machine learning explores the graph to suggest which biological targets might be worth pursuing for a given disease and which molecules might act on them, aiming to speed up the early stages of drug discovery.

The company gained attention when its system flagged baricitinib, an existing drug, as a possible treatment for COVID-19, which was later supported by clinical trials. It has formed partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms and developed its own programs. The platform combines AI with scientists who validate predictions in the lab.

item.title: Buoy Health
item.description: Buoy Health helps people decide what to do when they feel unwell. It asks a series of questions in a conversational flow, adapts based on the answers, and then provides possible explanations and a recommendation on the right level of care, such as self-care, a primary care visit, urgent care, or the emergency room. The aim is to reduce confusion and avoid unnecessary visits as well as delays in seeking urgent care.

item.title: Infermedica
item.description:
Infermedica builds medical decision support for patient-facing use. A person answers questions about symptoms in an adaptive interview, and the system estimates likely conditions and recommends a level of care, such as self-care, a doctor visit, or emergency services. Organizations embed this in their apps and websites.

The engine rests on a medical knowledge base maintained by physicians, combined with probabilistic reasoning and language models for understanding free text. Use cases include directing patients to the right service, preparing clinicians with an intake summary, and reducing unnecessary visits.

item.title: Insilico Medicine
item.description:
Insilico Medicine applies generative AI across the drug discovery process. PandaOmics analyzes biological data and literature to suggest disease targets, Chemistry42 designs novel molecules that bind to those targets, and other tools predict clinical trial outcomes and automate parts of the process. The idea is to cut the time and cost needed to move from an idea to a candidate drug.

The company has taken its approach into the clinic, with its own pipeline of drug candidates in areas such as fibrosis, cancer, and age-related diseases. One of its candidates, designed with the platform for a lung disease, advanced into human trials, which is regarded as an important test of whether AI-designed drugs can succeed. It also partners with pharmaceutical firms and sells software and services.

item.title: K Health
item.description:
K Health begins with a conversation. In the app, you describe your symptoms and answer questions, and the AI compares your information with a large database of anonymized patient records to suggest what similar patients turned out to have, along with possible next steps. The symptom checker is free and meant to help you decide what to do.

If you need care, you can move to a visit with a clinician through messaging or video, often within minutes, for common issues such as colds, infections, and prescriptions, and for ongoing care with a primary care provider. The company works with health systems and insurers in some places, and it offers programs for conditions like mental health and weight management. AI helps summarize information for doctors and speeds up triage.

item.title: Lunit
item.description:
Lunit applies deep learning to medical images. Insight CXR reads chest X-rays and flags abnormalities such as nodules and signs of tuberculosis, while Insight MMG reviews mammograms to help radiologists detect breast cancer. Radiologists see marked regions and probability scores to support their reading.

The company also works in oncology pathology. Its SCOPE tools analyze tissue slides to characterize the tumor environment, which helps predict how patients may respond to treatments such as immunotherapy. This feeds into drug development and personalized care.

item.title: Navina
item.description:
Navina addresses chart review. Before a patient visit, a clinician or care team would normally dig through records from different sources. Navina collects data from the electronic health record, outside providers, and claims, summarizes it, and highlights what matters, such as conditions that may be undocumented or screenings that are overdue.

That helps with both quality of care and risk adjustment, which affects payment under value-based contracts. Insights appear in the clinician’s workflow so they can act during the visit. Health systems and value-based care groups are the main customers.

item.title: Nuance DAX
item.description: DAX, short for Dragon Ambient eXperience, was developed by Nuance and later acquired by Microsoft. With patient consent, the system captures the conversation between clinician and patient, uses speech recognition and AI to turn it into a structured medical note in the format the clinician needs, and sends it to the electronic health record for review and signature. The goal is to cut the hours doctors spend on documentation and let them focus on patients.

item.title: Paige.AI
item.description:
Paige works on a part of medicine where AI could make a real difference: pathology, in which specialists examine tissue slides to diagnose cancer. Slides are scanned into very large digital images, and Paige’s algorithms analyze them, flagging areas that look suspicious and helping pathologists find cancer more efficiently and consistently. Its prostate cancer detection software was the first AI pathology tool to receive FDA clearance.

The company grew out of a collaboration with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and built a large collection of digitized slides paired with clinical and molecular data. It developed foundation models trained on millions of slides to support a broad range of cancer analysis tasks, and offers a platform for laboratories to deploy AI tools alongside digital pathology systems.

item.title: Suki AI
item.description:
Suki reduces the paperwork burden on doctors. With patient consent, its ambient system listens to the visit, converts the conversation into a structured clinical note in the specialty’s format, and places it in the electronic health record for review. Clinicians can also dictate or use voice commands to look up information, queue orders, and complete tasks hands-free.

The assistant extends beyond notes. It suggests billing codes based on the documentation, helps with information retrieval from the chart, and supports different specialties with tailored templates. Integration with major record systems is a priority, since adoption depends on fitting into existing workflows. Healthcare organizations use it to reduce time spent on documentation and clinician burnout.

item.title: Tempus AI
item.description:
Tempus builds a bridge between lab results and clinical decisions. It sequences tumors and other samples, combines the results with clinical data, and provides physicians with reports to help guide treatment choices, such as matching patients to targeted therapies or clinical trials. Over time, the company has assembled a large library of linked clinical and molecular data.

That data supports a second business: working with pharmaceutical companies. Tempus licenses de-identified data and builds models to help discover and develop drugs, find suitable patients for trials, and analyze outcomes. It has expanded through acquisitions into digital pathology with Paige and into radiology with the former Arterys platform, aiming to combine images, genomics, and clinical records into foundation models.

item.title: Flatiron Health
item.description:
Flatiron Health works in cancer care. Its electronic health record, OncoEMR, is used by many community oncology practices, and the data from those practices, once de-identified and curated, form a large real-world dataset. Researchers use it to study how treatments work outside clinical trials.

The company uses machine learning and human abstraction to turn unstructured notes into research-ready data. Biopharma companies use these datasets to understand patient populations, design trials, and support regulatory submissions. Products for clinics include tools for clinical workflows, billing, and trial matching.

item.title: Lyra Health
item.description:
Lyra provides employer-sponsored mental health care. Employees take an assessment and are matched with a provider from Lyra’s network of clinicians, with options for therapy, coaching, medication management, and digital programs. Employers pay for the benefit, so employees may have little or no out-of-pocket cost for a set number of sessions.

The company says it focuses on quality and outcomes by vetting providers and measuring progress. AI supports the matching process, helps clinicians with documentation, and powers a conversational tool offering support between sessions, while keeping clinicians involved in care.

item.title: Nabla
item.description:
Nabla works as a scribe in the exam room. During a visit, with consent, it captures the conversation and creates a structured note in the clinician’s preferred format, which they review and copy into the health record. It also drafts letters and patient instructions from the same encounter.

The company began in France and has expanded to the United States and elsewhere, with support for multiple languages and specialties. It emphasizes privacy, including not retaining audio after processing, and integrates with electronic health record systems.

item.title: PathAI
item.description:
PathAI works on digital pathology. Pathologists traditionally examine tissue slides under a microscope. With scanned slides, algorithms can highlight regions of interest, count cells, and measure biomarkers, which helps make reads more consistent. PathAI builds these tools and a platform for viewing and managing slides.

The company also supports pharmaceutical research. Its models analyze tissue from clinical trials to measure disease features and treatment responses, and it operates a laboratory service. The goal is to reduce variability and speed drug development.

item.title: Spring Health
item.description:
Spring Health provides employer-sponsored mental health care. Employees take an assessment, and the system recommends a path, from self-guided tools to coaching, therapy, or psychiatric care, with a care navigator to help. Providers are drawn from its network.

AI and measurement-based care play a role in matching and tracking progress. The company states that it collects outcomes data to adjust care. It serves employers, health plans, and other organizations.

Anyone in crisis should reach emergency services or a crisis line. Spring Health is sold to organizations, not directly to individuals. Alternatives include Lyra Health, Headspace Health, Talkspace, Modern Health, and Teladoc. Spring Health suits employees whose employers offer it.

item.title: Doximity
item.description:
Doximity is often described as LinkedIn for doctors. Physicians use it as a free directory and communication tool: they can find colleagues, send secure messages and faxes, and call patients using a number that shows the practice’s caller ID, all under a verified identity. Many of the country’s doctors have profiles, which makes it a convenient way to reach other clinicians for referrals and coordination.

The platform has added tools for clinical work. It provides medical news and journal feeds tailored to specialties, continuing education credits, telehealth video visits, and, increasingly, AI assistants for drafting letters, prior authorization appeals, and notes. A clinical reference tool answers questions drawn from medical sources. Doximity earns most of its revenue from pharmaceutical marketing and recruiting.
